Pain Associated With Ligamentous Laxity
 CORE
June 30, 2025
Thomas B. Hughes, Jr., MD, FAAOS (2020–present)
David Ring, MD, PhD (2025–present)
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the spectrum of ligamentous laxity as it pertains to the hand and wrist.
Identify specific disease states that are associated with ligamentous laxity.
Explain non-dissociative carpal alignment and kinematics (often referred to as instability).
Overview
Joint laxity is variable.
The degree of laxity is associated with variations in collagen and elastin.
Some of the variations are associated with laxity sufficiently notable to be named a disease
(eg, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome).
Other diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus may be associated with laxity.

Individuals present to a specialist for treatment if sensations related to their laxity become a
concern (a symptom).
Malalignment or laxity often is referred to as instability, which may be somewhat misleading.
Instability as a diagnosis or description may be unhelpful and ambiguous.
For example, abnormal carpal alignment may be observed in patients with an asymptomatic
wrist.
Individuals with a healthy wrist and normal alignment may present with pain.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Joint laxity and alignment depend on three key factors.
Bone geometry
Tension in ligaments under load
Function of musculotendinous units
Scoring systems that quantify laxity
Beighton score: joint hyperextensibility (mainly in orthopaedic discourse)
Score greater than 4 used as threshold for designating hyperlaxity
Brighton criteria: uses the Beighton score as one criterion and adds other factors, such as
symptoms (the number of joints that hurt) and skin, eye, and soft-tissue abnormalities;
standard in rheumatology discourse1 (Table 1).
Table 1 Brighton Tests and Criteria (n = 40)
Major criteria
1. Beighton score ≥4
2. Arthralgia in four or more joints for >3 mo
Minor criteria
1. Skin signs
2. Eye signs
3. Marfanoid habitus
4. Beighton score <4

5. Arthralgia in fewer than four joints
6. Dislocation/subluxation
7. Soft-tissue abnormalities
8. Varicose veins, hernia, prolapse
9. Presence of a first-degree relative
Combinations of diagnostic criteria
1. Two major
2. One major and two minor
3. Four minor
4. Two minor and one first-degree relative
Adapted with permission from Juul-Kristensen B, Røgind H, Jensen DV, Remvig L: Inter-examiner

Autoimmune disorders associated with laxity
SLE
Collagen diseases associated with laxity
Marfan syndrome
Heritable disorder linked to mutation of the FBN1 gene
Common findings of Marfan syndrome
Tall stature
Aortic root dilatation
Hypermobility
Optic lens dislocation
Striae
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Abnormalities of collagen fibrils and dermal elastic fibers
Hyperelastic skin in some variants
May have vascular manifestations
Joint hypermobility (Figure 1)
A higher percentage of abnormal collagen fibrils corresponds with greater laxity.

This suggests a spectrum of normal and abnormal joint mobility and that benign joint laxity
and hypermobility are associated with less severe forms of collagen abnormalities
compared with diseases such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Marfan syndrome.
The genetic variability of collagen, elastin, and the other components of soft-tissue restraints
to motion is incompletely understood.
A relatively low percentage of patients presenting for treatment of symptoms related to
laxity are never tested, making it difficult to understand the degree to which mutations, or
variations of normal, affect laxity.
Garcia-Elias et al2 noted an association between increased scaphoid rotation (from inherent
laxity) and ligament rupture.
Figure 1 Clinical photographs of a patient show criteria for a positive Beighton score for joint
laxity. A, Photograph of both arms shows elbow hyperextensibility greater than 10°. B,
Photograph of the hand and wrist shows small finger hyperextensibility. C, Photograph of the
hand and wrist shows ability to flex the thumb to touch the volar forearm. D, Photograph of both
legs show knee hyperextensibility. E, Photograph of the patient shows truncal flexibility.

(Reproduced from Wolf JM, Cameron KL, Owens BD: Impact of joint laxity and hypermobility on
the musculoskeletal system. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011;19[8]:463-471.)
Epidemiology
A Beighton score greater than 4 was noted in 5% of individuals donating blood.3
This suggests that benign hypermobility is an extreme on the range of normal joint motion
and not necessarily a systemic connective tissue disorder.
Hypermobility in athletes
264 healthy athletes screened4
13% of high school athletes had a Beighton score greater than 5
22% of females, 6% of males
Male athletes had Beighton scores of 5 or 6.
Female athletes had more than half of the abnormal Beighton scores of 6 to 9.
Wrist symptoms ascribed to laxity (occasionally referred to as carpal malalignment
nondissociative) is an uncommon diagnosis in a hand specialist’s office.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is relatively uncommon.
The prevalence of hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 20,000
individuals.5
SLE instability
A Beighton score greater than 4 is relatively common in patients with SLE (48% versus 15%
for a control group).6
Given that 160,000 to 320,000 individuals in the United States have SLE, this group is a very
small subset of the population.
Diagnoses Associated With Laxity
General Joint Laxity/Benign Joint Hypermobility Syndrome
Diagnosis made by rheumatologists7 (Resource 1)
Defined as presentation for specialty care for joint pain for more than 3 months in four or
more joints with laxity measurements above threshold.
Trapeziometacarpal Laxity
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:32 PM
AAOS | Pain Associated With Ligamentous Laxity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004102
5/21

A small subset of individuals with atraumatic laxity have symptoms at the trapeziometacarpal
(TMC) joint sufficient to bring them to a specialist. This is an uncommon diagnosis in a
specialist’s office.
A theory that laxity contributes to shear forces and osteoarthritis has been suggested.
The rationale is partly based on the observation that women present with symptoms from
TMC arthritis more often than men, and relaxing receptors are identified in the TMC joint
capsule.
Intuitively, the concept of laxity contributing to joint subluxation results in a lower surface
area of joint contact and, therefore, higher contact pressures and edge wear of the
metacarpal on the trapezium.
To date, this theory is not supported by experimental evidence.
Symptomatic laxity is common among individuals with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (Figure 2).
Radiographic findings in 24 individuals with Ehlers-Danlos with a mean age of 16 years8
66% subluxation
29% dislocation
16% joint space narrowing and osteophyte formation

Management
Reassurance/normalization that healthy lax joints occasionally may be uncomfortable.
Options for potential alleviation of symptoms (palliation)
Splint or temporary cast immobilization (Figure 3)
Rest or activity modifications
In many patients, painful motion is not dangerous and no alteration in natural history
results from protecting a painful lax joint; rather, immobilization is a form of symptomatic
management to improve pain or symptoms. This is important to convey to the patient to
avoid reinforcing unhealthy thoughts about pain (eg, fear of painful movement or worst-
case thinking).
Selective strengthening of the first dorsal interosseous and opponens pollicis
A retrospective review of 35 individuals who visited a hand therapist for assistance with
TMC arthrosis experienced a mean improvement of 18% in pain intensity and 19% in
capability (Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand questionnaire); however, the
study did not include a control intervention, and the improvements may be nonspecific.9

support to manage palmar carpal instability nondissociative. (Reproduced with permission from
Scott W. Wolfe, MD, New York, NY.)
Carpal Instability Nondissociative
Carpal Instability Nondissociative10 (Resources 2 and 3).
The term instability often is used to indicate malalignment or altered kinematics. The term
malalignment may be considered more accurate than instability.
So-called carpal instability dissociative is malalignment because of rupture and instability of
the stabilizing intercarpal ligaments (ie, the scapholunate interosseous).
Carpal instability nondissociative (CIND) does not involve rupture or insufficiency of an intrinsic
intercarpal ligament and is characterized by malalignment of the entire carpal row.
Originally described as a snapping wrist
Many patients with CIND will have discomfort only, without reproducible snapping.
Four major groups
Palmar CIND (CIND–volar intercalated segmental instability)
Dorsal CIND (CIND–dorsal intercalated segmental instability)
Combined CIND
Adaptive CIND
Fernandez Fok et al11 suggested adding a possible fifth group
CIND-traumatic
CIND results from traumatic disruption of the radiocarpal ligaments (or fracture of their
bony attachments), leading to palmar and dorsal CIND.
This group is difficult to classify.
Although it leads to an instability pattern between the carpal rows (similar to CIND), it is
associated with ligament injury (similar to carpal instability dissociative).
It is not a disease of ligamentous laxity but is mentioned here because it leads to a similar
pattern of instability between the carpal rows similar to that observed in CIND.

Palmar CIND
Most common CIND
Associated with benign joint hypermobility syndrome
Visible or palpable midcarpal sag and painful clunking
Routine observation of the catch-up clunk suggests more severe instability
Symptoms: painful clunking with ulnar deviation (eg, pouring liquids)
Physical examination
Typical midcarpal sag
Catch-up clunk—As the wrist is moved from radial to ulnar deviation, a dramatic clunk is
noted as the proximal row pops into extension from a volar intercalated segmental
instability position initially (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustrations of the wrist show ulnar deviation (large arrows). A, The catch-up clunk
(small arrow) occurs if the proximal carpal row suddenly shifts from flexion into extension as the
wrist translates from radial to ulnar deviation. B, With the wrist in ulnar deviation, the proximal
carpal is extended. The dashed outline indicates the extended position of the lunate.
(Reproduced from Wolfe SW, Garcia-Elias M, Kitay A: Carpal instability nondissociative. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 2012;20[9]:575-585.)
Pathomechanics
SEND FEEDBACK

Typically, in moving from radial to ulnar deviation, the palmar midcarpal ligament, flexor
carpi ulnaris, and extensor carpi ulnaris cause this to be a smooth motion.
If these are lax, the proximal row flexes, leading to the midcarpal volar sag (Figure 5).
The proximal row remains flexed until the triquetrohamate joint pushes the proximal row
into extension suddenly, leading to the clunk.

instability nondissociative shows volar sag (arrow) of the carpus. (Reproduced with permission
from Scott W. Wolfe, MD, New York, NY.)

Diagnostic imaging
Contralateral imaging or fluoroscopy may aid in the diagnosis.
Stress radiographs, including an anterior drawer stress view, may be helpful.
In the posttraumatic subset, MRI typically will demonstrate discontinuity of the
dorsoradiotriquetral ligament and the ulnar arcuate ligament.
This complex subset has elements of dissociative and non-dissociative instability.
No injury to a ligament is present directly between two carpal bones (such as the
scapholunate ligament or the lunotriquetral ligament, as is commonly described with
dissociative instability); therefore, no gapping is present between individual carpal
bones.
An injury to a radiocarpal ligament is present, leading to instability between the carpal
rows without individual carpal bone instability.
To date, little experimental data are available on the pathology, optimal management,
and outcomes for these types of conditions.
Dorsal CIND
Less common than palmar CIND
Symptoms of pain and clicking with gripping in supination
Dorsal displacement test (Figure 6)
The wrist is placed in flexion, ulnar deviation, and traction.
The scaphoid tubercle is pushed dorsally.
The proximal row and capitate translate dorsally, reproducing the pain.

Figure 6 Images show the dorsal displacement test. A, Illustration of the wrist shows the dorsal
capitate-displacement test. The examiner applies longitudinal traction and mild flexion to the
wrist while applying dorsally directed pressure to the scaphoid tubercle (arrow). This pressure
causes dorsal subluxation of the capitate and the proximal row. B, Lateral radiograph of the wrist
of a patient with dorsal carpal instability nondissociative demonstrates dorsal subluxation of the
capitate (top double arrow) on lunate and dorsal subluxation of the proximal row (lunate; bottom
double arrow) on the distal radius during the dorsal capitate-displacement stress test. C =
capitate, L = lunate, R = radius, S = scaphoid. (Panel A reproduced from Wolfe SW, Garcia-Elias M,
Kitay A: Carpal instability nondissociative. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[9]:575-585; panel B
reproduced with permission from Scott W. Wolfe, MD, New York, NY.)
Pathomechanics
The carpus typically is normally aligned at rest in patients with dorsal CIND.
The clunk in dorsal CIND is with capitate subluxation (compared with palmar CIND, in which
the clunk is from midcarpal relocation from a volar intercalated segmental instability
position).
Diagnostic imaging

Radiographs are normal.
Fluoroscopy aids in the diagnosis of dorsal CIND.
Dorsal capitate displacement stress test performed under fluoroscopy
Positive if dorsal pressure on the volar scaphoid in wrist flexion leads to capitate
subluxation and reproduces pain
Combined CIND
Described only in small case series
Midcarpal sag
Positive dorsal displacement test
Women affected more than men
Associated with benign joint hypermobility syndrome
Individuals presenting with symptoms often are athletes involved in gripping/striking sports
(volleyball, tennis, gymnastics).
Pathomechanics
Laxity of the volar and dorsal carpal ligaments
In radial deviation, the proximal row is flexed. With ulnar deviation, it clunks into extension
(similar to palmar CIND).
Extreme ulnar deviation leads to dorsal subluxation of the capitate.
Diagnostic imaging
Live fluoroscopy (cine) is critical, as are contralateral radiographs (or contralateral live
fluoroscopy).
Adaptive CIND
Secondary to the following:
Distal radius malunion with dorsal angulation
Unlocking of the scaphotrapeziotrapezoid joint via removal of the trapezium (as in TMC
arthroplasty)
Symptoms: snapping in ulnar deviation; may lead to midcarpal arthritis and pain.
Pathomechanics (theoretic)
Volar ligament laxity because of the malunion deformity
Proximal row extension and compensatory midcarpal flexion
Diagnostic imaging

Typically well demonstrated on radiographs (PA and lateral views) with comparison views of
the contralateral side.
Management
Information, reassurance, and gentle correction of common misconceptions about pain
Nonspecific symptom alleviation (palliative management)
Splinting
NSAIDS or acetaminophen
Surgical management
May be offered to individuals who are not satisfied with reassurance, proper understanding
of the problem, and palliative measures.
Soft-tissue procedures are unpredictable.
Partial wrist fusion may be an option.
Surgical management of palmar CIND
Soft-tissue reconstruction
Capsular shrinkage is associated with some improvement but only in the short-term.12
Multiple ligamentous reefings/advancements have been described with limited success.13
Advancement of the ulnar arm of the arcuate ligament resulted in the best outcomes
and only a 60% success rate.
Intercarpal fusion
Radiolunate fusion (Figure 7)

Figure 7 Radiographs of the wrist of a dart thrower who underwent radiolunate fusion, which
preserves motion and is a suitable treatment option for recalcitrant palmar carpal instability
nondissociative and combined carpal instability nondissociative. A, PA radiograph demonstrates
radiolunate fusion stabilized with the use of Kirschner wires. PA (B) and lateral (C) radiographs
demonstrate radiolunate fusion stabilized with the use of compression screws. D, PA radiograph
demonstrates radiolunate fusion after hardware removal. (Reproduced with permission from
Scott W. Wolfe, MD, New York, NY.)
Surgical management of dorsal CIND
Palmar ligament reefing and dorsal capsulodesis are treatment options for patients who
remain symptomatic.
Surgical management of combined CIND
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:32 PM
AAOS | Pain Associated With Ligamentous Laxity

18/21

Ligamentous reefing has been shown to be helpful; however, the results of surgical
management are far from predictable.
Surgical management of adaptive CIND
Corrective osteotomy of the radius
Results of surgical management of adaptive CIND tend to be more predictable than those for
other types of CIND.
This predictability may be because the pathophysiology (the malunion) is a discrete lesion
that can be corrected.
CIND-traumatic (posttraumatic CIND)
In posttraumatic patients (CIND-traumatic), early surgical treatment, consisting of
ligamentous repair and extended periods of immobilization with possible joint pinning,
may lead to good outcomes.14,15
Patients identified late usually require salvage with radiocarpal fusion.
To date, little experimental data are available on the pathology, optimal management,
and outcomes for these types of conditions.
Mark as Complete
